title: aham brahmasmi
tomorrow: one lesson that makes every other lesson make sense. real, or a scam?

segments.voice: Yesterday, aham brahmasmi hid the self like a razor in its case, and called it the footprint everything is found by. Today is this saying's last day, and a seer says it about himself.

The email arrives with a cheerful subject line: your ancestry results are in. A map lights up with places nobody at the family table ever mentioned. All at once, the story of you is older and wider than the one you grew up with. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a seer named Vamadeva goes much further than any map. He sits with one thought until it opens. Then he says it out loud. I was Manu. I was the sun. Is that a boast, a fever, or something else?
screen: `YOUR RESULTS ARE IN.` → `THE STORY IS WIDER THAN YOU.` → `I WAS MANU. I WAS THE SUN.` → `A BOAST, OR SOMETHING ELSE?`

segments.voice: The passage tells it like a waking up. In the beginning, it says, this was Brahman, and it knew itself only: I am Brahman. So it became all. Then the circle widens. Whoever among the gods woke up to this became that. So too among the seers. So too among people. Then one name. Seeing this, the seer Vamadeva understood: I was Manu, and the sun. Manu, in the tradition, is the ancestor of humankind. So Vamadeva isn't puffing up one small life. He's speaking from past its edges: the whole human family, and the light that shines on all of it. Look at who is on the list. Gods, seers, people. The text doesn't say this happened once, to one special man, and then the door closed. It names him, and it names the door: knowing. Then come the two words that keep the passage from staying in the old days. Even now. Even now, the text says, whoever knows I am Brahman becomes all this. Schools of Vedanta read aham brahmasmi in different ways, and the coming days give some of them a turn. This passage ends its part plainly. Even now.
screen: `IT KNEW ITSELF: I AM BRAHMAN.` · `GODS, SEERS, PEOPLE: WHOEVER WAKES.` · `I WAS MANU, AND THE SUN.` · then, large: `EVEN NOW.`

segments.voice: Sit easy and let the breath find its own pace. On one out-breath, say two words softly, out loud if you can: even now. Then let them go, and listen to the quiet after them, which is also now.
Aham brahmasmi: I am Brahman. Vamadeva knew it as I was Manu, and the sun, and the text says the knowing still opens, even now.
Your line: aham brahmasmi, not only back then, but even now. Eight days with one saying, complete.

howItsDone: In Vedanta study, the Brihadaranyaka's passage on Vamadeva is read with a teacher and a commentary, and aham brahmasmi is taught as one of the great sayings of the Upanishads.

fork.setup: a kid at camp says the old sages were basically superheroes, and none of that could happen to normal people now. what does this passage say?
options: right: the old sages had a power ordinary people don't have.
even now: whoever knows I am Brahman becomes all this.
it's only a story about the past, so it says nothing about now.
fork.reveal: the passage lists gods, seers and people, names Vamadeva, then adds 'even now'. it doesn't lock the knowing in the past.

original.note: Sanskrit: I am Brahman. aham (I) + brahma (Brahman) + asmi (am), from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: a seer bragging that he's God.
what it means: a waking up the passage opens to gods, seers and people, and says still happens even now.
what a scholar hears: aham manur abhavam suryash cha, I was Manu and the sun, read as Vamadeva's knowing; Vedanta's schools interpret it differently.
recall: the footprint everything is found by

chat.meaning: In the Brihadaranyaka, knowing comes first: it knew itself only, I am Brahman, and so it became all.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.meaning: a long, early Upanishad where aham brahmasmi appears

Vamadeva.meaning: a seer who said: I was Manu, and the sun

Manu.meaning: in the tradition, the ancestor of humankind

Brahman.meaning: the one reality the Upanishads point to

Vedanta.meaning: the schools that read the Upanishads closely
